terms.definition: The long, stable stage of a star's life when it fuses hydrogen into helium in its core. Stars spend roughly 90% of their lives here.
terms.function: The star's default state — the balance of gravity and fusion pressure that keeps it steady.

terms.definition: The balance between gravity pulling a star inward and the pressure of fusion energy pushing it outward, so the star keeps a constant size.
terms.whereItIs: Every layer of the star, from core to photosphere
terms.whyItMatters: It is the reason a star can shine for billions of years without collapsing or expanding.

terms.definition: Merging light atomic nuclei into heavier ones with a release of energy — hydrogen into helium in main-sequence cores.
The visible surface of the star, where light finally escapes into space — about 5,772 K for the Sun.
terms.whereItIs: The outermost visible layer of the star
terms.whyItMatters: Its color is the direct reading of the star's surface temperature.

terms.definition: The layer inside the star where energy travels outward as light, constantly absorbed and re-emitted — the slow, crawling middle section of the star's interior.
terms.function: Transfers energy from core to outer shell.

terms.definition: The outer shell of the star where hot gas rises and cooler gas sinks in boiling cells, carrying energy to the surface.
terms.whereItIs: The outermost interior layer, beneath the photosphere
terms.whyItMatters: The churning makes the surface look grainy and mixes the star's gas.
